findings.text: Guest execution is globally visible for both non-VHE and host-extensions modes, each taking a virtual CPU and returning an exit reason for host handling.

Processor, timer and debug state transfer helpers are globally visible, covering non-VHE full save and restore, host-extensions shared and return handling, timer trap enable and disable, and debug direction switches.
Protected memory helpers are globally visible, covering cache refill from host to hypervisor with a minimum page guarantee and host to guest page donation for a single page.

Non-VHE run request resolves host and hypervisor CPUs from host context, rejects unresolvable targets, validates streaming extension quiescence for protected executions, then either flushes plus runs plus synchronizes the hypervisor copy or runs the host CPU directly with floating point ownership transferred around execution, reporting status in the incoming operand slot.
Synchronization request refreshes the loaded hypervisor CPU only when such a CPU exists and is outside protected mode; otherwise it returns without effect.

Donation request carries host and guest frame numbers in two operand slots, proceeds only for a loaded protected CPU with successful cache refill, attempts single page donation, and reports numeric status in the first operand slot.

Host pointer resolution moves the pointer into hypervisor address space. Under protected mode the loaded hypervisor CPU must exist and link back to the same host CPU, else both results become empty. Outside protected mode the hypervisor result is always empty. An interrupt interface form first derives the host CPU from its embedded controller state, then applies identical validation.

Non-VHE execution moves through host capture, guest install, repeated entry, and host restore. Host capture records the running CPU and preserves processor and debug state behind ordering barriers. Guest install activates translation, traps and virtualized devices. Entry repeats while exit repair asks for retry. Restore reverses device, translation, processor and ownership steps and clears the running marker before returning the exit reason.

Host-extensions execution masks interrupts around an inner run. The inner run transfers floating point ownership inward, captures host shared state, enables traps, installs guest state, repeats entry while exit repair asks for retry, then captures guest state, disables traps, restores host state, orders system writes, and transfers floating point ownership outward with legacy exception preservation when the guest retains registers.

Non-VHE trap controls are paired: activation preserves host debug configuration, installs guest trap and debug configuration with common and capability controls, and selects guest vectors; deactivation restores host debug configuration, common and capability controls, host flags and host vectors.

Interrupt save and restore select generation-specific handling. One generation uses dedicated state plus private state paths. The other applies only when a global CPU interface capability is enabled, pairing activation with restore on entry and save with deactivation on exit.

When counting virtualization is present, entry disables host enables and enables guest enables, exit does the reverse, and entry reports whether either mask was nonzero so exit work can be skipped when both are empty.
When counting virtualization is absent, guest switch yields false and host switch has no effect, indicating no counter ownership work exists.
Exit dispatch uses a protected table for protected CPUs and the standard hypervisor table otherwise, chosen fresh for each exit repair.

A protected guest observed in 32-bit mode is deemed invalid: its initialized mark is cleared, only the asynchronous error indication of the exit reason is kept, an illegal exception indication is forced, and shared exit repair still runs. This prevents trusting the host to detect the transition.
Non-VHE processor save covers first level, shared, user and return groups; restore covers the same groups with identification and affinity seeding first level restoration.

Host timer restoration allows physical timer and counter, with a shifted encoding on hypervisor-enhanced hosts. Guest programming denies physical timer, allows physical counter only for protected guests or zero physical offset, shifts masks likewise when needed, and traps virtual timer and counter only under broken offset handling with nonzero virtual offset.
Host-extensions debug direction switches delegate directly to shared common handling without extra local policy.

Host-extensions activation merges stored and computed hypervisor controls, reloads a direct physical timer compare value from memory when offset support and a direct mapping coincide, enables capability traps, and selects guest vectors.

Computed hypervisor controls pass through unchanged without nesting. With nesting the code records hypervisor context entry, forces nesting and translation bits, publishes the guest control view through hardware or emulated backing, programs nested backing addresses with low-bit inheritance, applies configuration masks and guest exclusions, suppresses delay settings without their master enable, and forbids simultaneous hypervisor context and mapping flags.

Host-extensions deactivation restores fixed host flags, writes back the live direct timer compare value and reapplies counter offset when a direct mapping and nonzero offset coincide, orders execution before translation regime change on mitigated parts, disables capability traps, and picks host vectors from kernel mapping state.
Host-extensions exit repair synchronizes processor views, applies nested adjustment for nested guests, then runs shared repair with the standard table; its boolean outcome decides re-entry.

Nested adjustment remaps first level thread and handler modes to second level equivalents when entry was in hypervisor context, republishes latest hypervisor controls from hardware or emulated backing, and requires the recorded context flag to match the architectural context test.
Host-extensions processor handling keeps host save and restore to shared state only, while guest save and restore add return state.

Cache refill guarantees a minimum hypervisor page count by admitting host pages through translation, consuming a working copy of the host cache and writing the remainder back. The CPU wrapper pairs the embedded hypervisor cache with the linked host cache counts and storage.

Donation validates that the host page is owned and the guest slot is empty with adequate table cache, encodes guest ownership metadata for the host range, and creates a single page second stage mapping as owned with full permissions.
Donation acquires host ownership before guest ownership and releases in reverse order, holding both across all validation and mapping steps including early failure exits.

A virtual CPU carries architecture context with processor register file and control copies, interrupt CPU state with generation-specific members, timer mappings, performance event masks for host and guest, protection flags and page cache linkage; host context additionally tracks the currently running virtual CPU.
A hypervisor virtual CPU embeds a full virtual CPU and links back to its host virtual CPU; donation derives the owning virtual machine from this link and refill pairs the two caches through it.
Protected run entry with streaming extension activity asserted on capable hardware is rejected as host misbehavior before any flush or execution.

On parts needing speculative translation mitigation, guest address controls must be installed only after second stage enablement with ordering barriers, and removal must disable translation walks before re-enabling the memory system, in exact opposite order.

Entering the guest with interrupts masked by priority would block host wakeup except via guest exceptions, so entry raises the priority mask with synchronization and exit lowers it; host-extensions entry relies on interrupt masking plus synchronization for hypervisor interrupt forwarding.
Hypercall operands and status use general register slots of host context: first operand and status share one slot, donation adds a second operand in the next slot.
Forced invalid exit encoding keeps the asynchronous error bit of the original reason and sets illegal exception semantics.
